name: CUDA-L1
language: CUDA (kernels generated by a contrastive reinforcement-learning LLM) with Python
baseline: KernelBench PyTorch reference implementations (default PyTorch eager, which calls cuDNN/cuBLAS), torch.compile, torch.compile reduce-overhead and CUDA Graph
workload: 250 KernelBench PyTorch workloads (levels 1 to 3) evaluated on A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20 and L40.
claimed_speedup: README table, mean speedup vs Default: A100 3.12x, 3090 2.51x, H100 3.85x, H20 2.38x, L40 3.13x; vs Torch Compile on A100 2.77x; vs Torch Compile RO 2.88x; vs CUDA Graph 2.81x; maximum single-task speedup 120x.
hardware: NVIDIA A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20, L40; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Kernels are released as per-GPU code snippets (JSON, a separate version for each device: A100, 3090, H100, H20, L40), each specialised to a KernelBench task. Not a library.
caveats: The README itself reports that RL exploited timing and caching reward hacks; they added stream timing sync and removed caching, but more hacks may remain. KernelBench reference code is naive eager PyTorch with many small ops, so much of the speedup is fusion rather than a better cuDNN-class kernel. Baselines are not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen; a 'cuDNN backend flags' comparison is listed as done in the to-do list but no numbers were read for it.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels (neighbour of CUDA-L2), then CUDA-L1 README evaluation tables

verification.tier_reason: README tables give first-party mean/max speedups over KernelBench PyTorch eager, torch.compile and CUDA Graph references on five GPUs, with per-task code and scores released in optimized_cuda_code/*.json; no software versions, flags or host CPU, and the released data do not support the headline maximum, so C with the claim corrected.
verification.notes: Claim overstated: headline 120x/3.12x rests on degenerate zero-output tasks and a top score whose released code equals the reference (correctness/measurement problem worth recording; consider wrong category since output is RL-generated per-task PyTorch snippets, not a library). Metadata confirmed via github.com: MIT, 323 stars, 109 forks, not archived/fork, last commit 2025-11-03 ('add lazyness check in eval'); LICENSE text says 'Copyright (c) 2021 ShannonAI'. arxiv.org and emergentmind.com blocked.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence (MQF precedent, timing work that is never done): the released a100/h100/3090/h20/l40 result files still hold LazyMatmul solutions for task 1/9 (17.8-107.9x) that never compute the output in the timed region, L2/80 returns a cached zero tensor and L2/83 (110.8x) runs on a task whose output is always zero; issue #12 reports a false 600x from the same bypass (open), and the eval script's 2025-11-03 laziness check was not followed by re-scored results. Released H100 L1 data give a median 1.177x vs the paper's headline. Real-CUDA solutions only: median ~1.14x, geomean ~1.34x on A100 (derived). Also RL-generated per-task snippets, not a library.

name: OxiBLAS
baseline: OpenBLAS (version and thread count not stated)
workload: GEMM throughput for square sizes 64 to 1024 (f32 and f64) on an Apple M3 and an Intel Xeon E5-2623 v4, README tables from the repo's criterion benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: Rust (MSRV 1.85); optimization flags not stated; NEON micro-kernels on M3, AVX2 on Xeon
hardware: Apple M3 (NEON, benchmarked 2025-12-28) and Intel Xeon E5-2623 v4 @ 2.60GHz Broadwell-EP (benchmarked 2025-12-27)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust BLAS and LAPACK with sparse, tensor and iterative-solver extras, for the SciRS2 ecosystem; Rust API only (the README says the oxiblas-ffi crate is retired), so not directly callable from C++. Optional Rayon parallelism.
caveats: Mostly parity: the same tables show 80-95% of OpenBLAS at several sizes (Xeon f64 512x512 is 80%, 128x128 90%) and the large f32 gap is on one M3 size class, where OpenBLAS may not be using its best Apple kernels. OpenBLAS version, thread settings and compiler flags are not given, and the numbers are first-party. Only 4 commits visible on main (release snapshots).
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'BLAS library written in Rust OR C++ OR Mojo faster than OpenBLAS 2026'; opened README

Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'OxiBLAS pure Rust BLAS beat OpenBLAS Apple Silicon github cool-japan' (Rust leads); opened the repo README and crates/oxiblas-benchmarks README

verification.tier_reason: First-party README tables vs OpenBLAS on named CPUs (Xeon E5-2623 v4, Apple M3) with public Criterion code (crates/oxiblas-benchmarks/benches/comparison.rs) and bench profile (opt-level 3, thin LTO), but rustc version, RUSTFLAGS/target-cpu and the OpenBLAS version/threads are not stated, so not A.
verification.notes: Ratios in the record match the README, but the absolute Gf/s values it quoted are the README's mislabelled numbers (8x too high), so claimed_speedup was rewritten in Gelem/s. Shortcoming worth recording: baseline-only allocation in the comparison bench and inflated GFLOPS labels. Apache-2.0, 43 stars, last commit 2026-08-06 confirmed; confirmed ndarray-linalg 0.18 default feature enables ndarray/blas, so .dot() does reach OpenBLAS.
verification.reject_reason: Evidence invalid by the project's own audit: TODO.md says the README's 80-172% OpenBLAS ratios have 'no reproducible backing — reads as fabricated/cherry-picked' and the crate README dropped them (the root README still shows them); the bench also links oxiblas-blas's #[no_mangle] cblas_sgemm/cblas_dgemm into the same binary as OpenBLAS, so the 'OpenBLAS' column may have called OxiBLAS itself; Gf/s labels were 8x too high. Same family as the fabricated-evidence precedents.

name: ra_prng (ra_core singleblock)
workload: Wall-clock generation of batches of up to 255 words (K=255) and single-word reinitialise-per-call use (K=1), plus long streams, comparing the array-permutation generator ra_core_singleblock/orbit against xoshiro256** and Philox4x32-10 with the code inlined the same way.
claimed_speedup: README table (2026-09-12): ra_core_singleblock K=255 real throughput 20018.1 MB/s vs Xoshiro256** K=255 2937.2 MB/s and Philox4x32-10 K=255 1007.9 MB/s ('~19.9x faster than Philox and ~6.8x faster than Xoshiro256**'); at K=1, 307.3 MB/s vs xoshiro 544.8 MB/s, i.e. slower.
tradeoffs: C library with a roughly 2 KB state (two 256-entry arrays permuting each other); explicitly not cryptographic; the fast mode only pays off for batches (K=255) and loses to xoshiro256** at K=1; the orbit (long-stream) mode is about 3.2x slower than xoshiro256** per the README.
caveats: Own benchmark by the author, in a regime (K=255 batches, steady-state loop cost shown as '~0.00 ns/word') chosen where the generator wins; the README documents an earlier benchmark fairness bug (reference generators were un-inlined) and a retracted earlier claim, so numbers may keep moving. Statistical testing is thin (PractRand clean to 8 GB for K=1/K=255, to 128 GB for ra_prng2; BigCrush for ra_prng2). CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is a non-commercial share-alike license and not an OSI software license, so the code is reference only. Not a C++ library per se (C API callable from C++).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng?l=c&o=desc&s=stars (ooalahhq/ra_prng listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.
GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/prng?l=c (listed as ooalahhq/ra_prng); README opened directly
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page github.com/topics/prng (C) listed ooalahhq/ra_prng; README and commit history opened.

verification.tier_reason: Benchmark code (bench_release.c), GCC 13.2.0, -O3 -march=native and the i3-1115G4 CPU are all stated, but the singleblock K=1/K=255 timings measure a call whose output is discarded (only init and call overhead remain), so they are not valid evidence. The valid first-party rows show no win over xoshiro256**.
verification.notes: Reject on the MQF precedent (timed a no-op): checked ra_core.c lines ~374-430 and bench_release.c; outputs are only reachable through fwrite(raw_stream), which the benchmark sets to NULL, and ra_core_singleblock returns the key. Not compiled (no builds allowed); the reasoning rests on the source plus the README's own ~0.00 ns/word generate column. Metadata confirmed: 5 stars, 0 forks, 215 commits, last commit 2026-09-12, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence (MQF precedent, timing a no-op): bench_release.c passes raw_stream=NULL and ra_core_singleblock returns the key, so the generated output is never consumed; the 20 GB/s headline measures init plus call overhead (README shows generate ~0.00 ns/word). Real orbit rows are 3.2x slower than xoshiro256**.

name: SIMD-MT
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::uniform_real_distribution, lrand48, drand48, POSIX random)
workload: Google Benchmark per-call latency of next() for header-only SIMD-friendly Mersenne Twister engines with 8 interleaved streams (IRNG for integers, FRNG for floats) versus a reference scalar MT, std::mt19937 and libc generators.
claimed_speedup: README (Travis CI run 2020-05-18): BM_IRNG_next 2.32 ns, BM_FRNG_next 2.31 ns, reference MT next 3.45 ns, std::mt19937 6.33 ns, std::uniform_real_distribution 6.84 ns (about 2.7x faster than std::mt19937 for integers and 3.0x faster than std::uniform_real_distribution for floats, derived from page data).
hardware: Travis CI VM, '2 X 2800.17 MHz CPU s' (no CPU model), L2 1024 KiB, L3 33792 KiB
tradeoffs: Header-only; compiler-vectorized loops over 8 interleaved MT streams, so output is not the same sequence as std::mt19937 and the state is 8x larger; alignment and stream count are template parameters.
caveats: Only one CI log in the README: compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated, and the author says the edge over the reference implementation is smaller on his laptop. Numbers are per-call latency in a microbenchmark loop. Last commit 2020-05-18.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/mersenne-twister?l=c%2B%2B (SIMD-MT listed); opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

verification.tier_reason: The README shows a first-party Travis CI Google Benchmark run (benchmark/src/bench.cpp, built with g++-7 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, -Wall -march=native) against std::mt19937. The CPU model is not stated (only '2 X 2800.17 MHz', L3 33792 KiB), so it cannot be A. The claim is downgraded because the generator is not actually MT19937; the tier stays C.
verification.notes: A same-generator check was done as asked. The SIMD path equals its scalar reference, but both carry the 0x8000000 mask typo (also found in a common competitive-programming RNG template), so the 'Mersenne Twister' timed against std::mt19937 is a different, non-linear generator. Unlike SIMDxorshift, the bug does not reduce work per output, so I kept the entry with the correctness bug recorded. Reject instead if the SIMDxorshift/stb-zip precedent is read as 'computes a different function than the named baseline'. Metadata matches the record: MIT, 0 stars, 21 commits, last commit 2020-05-18, not a fork.
verification.reject_reason: Computes a different generator than the MT19937 it is named for and timed against: mt.hpp and its reference.hpp use upper mask 0x8000000 (should be 0x80000000) and combine with +, so outputs differ from real MT19937 from output 2 (1847 of the first 2000 differ, verifier's Python check). The 2.7x over std::mt19937 compares different functions. Same precedent as SIMDxorshift and stb-zip (fast path computing a different function than the named baseline).

stars_or_usage: 125 stars; used by Yandex ClickHouse (per README)
tradeoffs: Needs Haswell+ AVX2 (AVX-512 for fastest path). xorshift128+ fails BigCrush per the README.
caveats: README gives no CPU model or compiler flags. Baseline is scalar xorshift128+, not xoshiro or mt19937; weak statistical quality.
name: SIMDxorshift
workload: Filling a 5000-element array of 32-bit random numbers (19 kB), cycles per element
claimed_speedup: scalar 3.63 cycles/op vs AVX 2.21, AVX variant two 1.88, AVX-512 variant two 1.47 cycles/op
found_via: GitHub: 'SIMD AVX2 AVX-512 vectorized xoshiro random number generator C++ library github'
WebSearch: arXiv new PRNG C++ faster than xoshiro256++ SIMD vectorized random number generator

verification.tier_reason: README shows first-party fillarray output: scalar xorshift128+ 3.63 cycles/value vs AVX-512 two-stream 1.47 (AVX2 2.21, AVX2 two-stream 1.88) on 'a Skylake-X processor'. Benchmark code (benchmark/fillarray.c) and Makefile flags are public, but the compiler is unnamed (plain $(CC)) and no exact CPU model is given, so not A.
verification.notes: Numbers match README exactly. Last commit 2020-07-22 (>3 years), so abandoned; Apache-2.0 confirmed via LICENSE file.
verification.reject_reason: Fast path computes a different generator than the scalar baseline it is timed against: avx_xorshift128plus/avx512_xorshift128plus set s1 from part2 instead of the old part1 (src/simdxorshift128plus.c vs src/xorshift128plus.c, checked 2026-10-01), so part1 is never read and the state effectively collapses to one word. Same precedent as stb-zip (fast path computing a different checksum).
